name: Manypenny Agreement of 1876 with the Sioux, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho, enacted by the Act of February 28, 1877 (Black Hills cession)
aka: Agreement with the Sioux, Arapaho and Northern Cheyenne, 1876
nations: Lakota, Dakota and Nakota (Oceti Sakowin) of the Great Sioux Reservation
promises: The nations were to give up the Black Hills portion of the Great Sioux Reservation and their hunting rights in the unceded territory of the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty.
In return the United States would provide subsistence rations until the people were able to support themselves.

The reservation boundary was redrawn, adding some 900,000 acres to the north while removing nearly everything between the 103rd and 104th meridians, including the Black Hills (as the Supreme Court described the 1877 Act).

breaches.what: Congress enacted the 1876 'agreement' into law although it had been signed by only about 10% of adult Sioux men, not the three-fourths that Article 12 of the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty required for any cession. The Supreme Court said the Act had the effect of abrogating the Fort Laramie treaty.

breaches.what: The Supreme Court held that the 1877 Act was a taking of the Black Hills that required just compensation, and affirmed the Court of Claims award of interest at an annual rate of 5% on the principal of $17.1 million from 1877. It upheld the Court of Claims holding that the uncertain promise of rations was not adequate consideration for the Black Hills.

breaches.what: The Oglala Sioux Tribe's president said the Black Hills are not for sale, and the Sioux nations continue to refuse the award and ask for the land.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Oglala Sioux Tribe President Frank Star Comes Out, as reported by the Christian Science Monitor

source.title: When $1 billion isn't enough. Why the Sioux won't put a price on land.

landTaken: The Black Hills, which the Supreme Court described as an area of well over 7 million acres, and the hunting rights in the unceded territory (448 U.S. 371).
compensation: Rations only at the time. The Court of Claims awarded interest at an annual rate of 5% from 1877 on $17.1 million, the 1877 value of the Black Hills, affirmed by the Supreme Court in 1980; the Sioux nations have refused it (448 U.S. 371; Christian Science Monitor, 2023).
today: The award remains unaccepted and held in trust; it was reported in 2023 to exceed $1 billion (Christian Science Monitor, 2023-06-28). The same events are recorded under the 1868 treaty in kappler-1006.

nationVoice.summary: Its president said in 2023 that the Black Hills are not for sale.

openQuestions: The Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho share in this cession (their hunting rights under the 1868 treaties) has no finding recorded here.
The Christian Science Monitor article was opened on 2026-11-07 and quotes President Star Comes Out directly.

Audit 2026-11-08: the interest is given as the opinion states it ('the annual rate of 5%'); the earlier 'simple' was not in the opinion. The rations finding is now in the Court's words ('adequate consideration').

plain.promised: The nations were to give up the Black Hills and their hunting rights in the unceded territory; in return the United States would provide subsistence rations until the people were able to support themselves.
plain.happened: Congress made the agreement law in 1877, though only about 10% of adult Sioux men had signed, not the three-fourths the 1868 treaty required. The Supreme Court held in 1980 that this was a taking requiring just compensation.
plain.today: The award, $17.1 million plus 5% a year from 1877, remains unaccepted and held in trust; it was reported in 2023 to exceed $1 billion. The Sioux nations ask for the land.
